texts.preamble: Kanhaiya Lal vs The State Of M.P. on 6 February, 2018 Cr.R. 280/ 2000 1 High Court Of Judicature Madhya Pradesh, Jabalpur Single Bench: Hon'ble Shri Justice Subodh Abhyankar, J Criminal Revision No. 280/2000 (Kanhaiya Lal Vs. State of M.P.) -------------------------------------------------------------------------
texts.facts: In brief the facts of the case are that on 09.05.1994, Food Inspector visited the milk dairy of the applicant Kanhaiya Lal situated at Dwarika Nagar, Lalmati, Jabalpur. After disclosing his identity, he purchased 750 ml of milk and as per the due procedure the same was sent for examination to the Public Analyst for his report, wherein the milk was found to be adulterated. Subsequently, a private complaint was filed by the Food Inspector before the JMFC and the JMFC, after recording the evidence recording conviction against the applicant as mentioned above and being aggrieved of the same, criminal appeal was preferred by the applicant before the lower appellate Court, which was also dismissed.
texts.arguments: 3. Learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that in the present case, he has been convicted of an offence punishable under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (hereinafter referred to as Kanhaiya Lal vs The State Of M.P. on 6 February, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/133520962/ 1 'Act'), which provides a detailed procedure to be followed to prosecute a person and certain mandatory provisions of the aforesaid Act has not been followed by the learned Judge of the Trial Court, which have been over-looked by the learned appellate Court as well. 4. Learned counsel for the applicant has submitted in the petition that the samples were taken on 9.5.1994. The report of the Public Analyst was received on 20.06.1994 and the matter was sent to the Central Government for obtaining consent to file complaint and the consent was provided on 23.09.1996, which is inordinate delay in prosecuting the applicant. No explanation has been provided for such an inordinate delay. On this ground, learned counsel for the applicant submits that the complaint itself should be thrown out of the Court. It is further submitted that the documents filed along with the complaint have not been proved as only photocopies have been filed by the complainant, which have been exhibited without formal proof and it is further submitted that the applicant was not issued requisite notice as provided under Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which has led to serious prejudice to him. So far as the right to get the sample examination is concerned, it is further submitted that after the applicant submitted the application on 30.01.1999 to get the sample examined through the Central Food Laboratory, he also deposited requisite fees for the same and the orders in this behalf were passed by the learned J.M.F.C. on 17.03.1999 to produce the samples to be sent for examination by Central Food Laboratory but samples were not brought to the Court on 22.03.1999, 24.03.1999, 5.4.1999 and the samples were produced only on 12.04.1999 whereas under Section 13(2-A) it is provided that when an application is made to the Court under sub-section (2), the Court shall require the Local (Health) Authority to forward the part or parts of the sample kept by the said Authority and upon such requisition being made, the said Authority shall forward the part or parts of the sample to the Court within a period of five days from the date of receipt of such requisition. Thus, it is submitted that non-compliance of Section 13(2-A) of the Act has vitiated the entire trial and on this ground also, the impugned orders are liable to be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. It is further submitted that the trial Court has framed charges against the applicant under Section 2(a)(d) of the Act and as such no specific charges have been framed against him which has led to the prejudice against him as he could not lead the evidence to counter charges under which ultimately he was convicted.
